title: Harriet Tubman
hookLine: she escaped slavery and went back, again and again, guided by prayer

cards: She has made it. After nights of walking, hiding in woods and following the North Star, she crosses into a free state. She said later that she looked at her hands to see if she was the same person.
There was such a glory over everything, she said, she felt like she was in heaven. Then the thought arrives: her family is still back there. Her brothers, her parents, her friends.
She is free, and she is alone. Plenty of stories would end at the border. This one turns around and walks back toward the danger.

teach.h: A HEAD WOUND, AND VIVID DREAMS.
teach.b: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland.
As a girl, she was struck in the head by a heavy weight an overseer threw at someone else, and for the rest of her life she had spells and vivid dreams that she understood as God speaking to her.
After her escape, she went back into slave country again and again, bringing out family members and others by night along what people called the Underground Railroad.
She was remembered as saying she never lost a passenger. How did she do it?

teach.h: PRAYING LIKE TALKING TO A FRIEND.
teach.b: She prayed, constantly and plainly, the way you'd talk to a friend.
People who knew her said she spoke with God as someone she trusted completely, moving when she felt led and waiting when she felt warned. And people gave her a name from scripture: Moses.
In Exodus, God says to Moses, in the King James Bible: "Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt."
And Moses carries the message to Pharaoh: "Let my people go." Enslaved people sang about that very story, and tradition says Tubman used songs like Go Down, Moses as signals that she was near.
Why does the name land so hard? Because Moses had already gotten out of Egypt, and was sent back. That's Tubman exactly.
The freedom she found was never meant to stay hers alone.

how: Some churches tell Tubman's story in services on freedom and justice, and spirituals like Go Down, Moses are still sung in worship.

games.q: you've just crossed into a free state after nights on the run. your family is still enslaved. what do you do?
o: settle down and start a new life.
go back into danger to bring them out.
write letters and hope for the best.
games.why: Tubman went back, again and again, praying the whole way. she was remembered as saying she never lost a passenger.

practice: Think of a place you've gotten out of, a hard season, a habit, a grief, and of someone who is still in it.
Let their face come clearly, and turn toward them in your mind, the way she turned at the border, asking what one small thing would help them find the way.
If you pray, ask to be led, as she did; if you don't, keep looking back with kindness.

wordCard.voice: Harriet Tubman. She escaped slavery, went back for others again and again, and prayed the whole way. People called her Moses.

orig.note: Hebrew: Moshe, Moses — the name Tubman's people gave her, after the one sent back to Egypt to lead his people out.

carryVoice: Your line: the moses of her people. Getting out was only half of her story. Nine hundred twenty days in.
